subject: Stephen Skinner (b. 22 March 1948, Sydney) — reception, criticism, and the contested continuity thesis
disciplineNote: Every claim below carries a source and a provenance class. Disputes are reported as positions with named holders and are not adjudicated. No operative text is transcribed anywhere in this slice; editions are described at the level of procedure type, structural anatomy and completeness only.

provenanceClasses.peer-reviewed-journal: review or article in an academic journal with editorial oversight
provenanceClasses.academic-reference-work: entry in an academically edited reference work (here: a Brill dictionary preprint self-archived by its author)
provenanceClasses.university-repository: thesis record in a university's institutional repository
provenanceClasses.scholar-blog: review on the personal blog of a credentialed scholar/librarian publishing under his own name
provenanceClasses.practitioner-venue: occult-community magazine, blog or forum review
provenanceClasses.bibliographic-survey: independent para-academic bibliographic survey, accessed via mirror (provenance caveat recorded)
provenanceClasses.self-reported: traceable only to Skinner's own site, his publisher's copy, or a page he controls

whatSkinnerClaims.summary: Demonstrable technical continuity of magical TECHNIQUES AND IMPLEMENTS — not merely motifs — from the Graeco-Egyptian magical papyri (PGM/PDM, 2nd c. BCE–5th c. CE), via Byzantine Greek Solomonic manuscripts (above all the Hygromanteia / Magical Treatise of Solomon, 6th–16th c.), into the Latin and English Solomonic grimoires (13th–19th c.), especially the Clavicula Salomonis. The claim is that magic persisted as a 'spiritual technology' whose operational rationale stayed recognisably Graeco-Egyptian, with the major changes confined to the theological character of the spirits addressed, the nomina, and the materia magica.

doctoralBasis.claim: The thesis was examined and the PhD in Classics awarded by the University of Newcastle (NSW, Australia); the two Techniques volumes are the published, expanded halves of the dissertation.
doctoralBasis.thesisTitle: Magical techniques and implements present in Graeco-Egyptian magical papyri, Byzantine Greek Solomonic manuscripts and European grimoires: transmission, continuity and commonality (the technology of Solomonic magic)

sources.cite: University of Newcastle (Australia) institutional repository, record uon:13943, https://ogma.newcastle.edu.au/vital/access/manager/Repository/uon:13943 (mirrored at openresearch.newcastle.edu.au, thesis id 29020349)
Wikipedia, 'Stephen Skinner (writer)', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Skinner_(writer) — PhD in Classics, Newcastle, 2014; article relies partly on Skinner's own site for career detail

publications.title: Techniques of Graeco-Egyptian Magic
publications.publisher: Golden Hoard Press, Singapore, 2014; US trade edition Llewellyn
publications.whatItContains: Technique-level anatomy of the PGM corpus: the procedures are separated and tabulated into 40+ named technique categories using the papyri's own Greek and Demotic technical vocabulary (types of evocation, protection, divination, binding, familiar-spirit acquisition, etc.), with tables of spirit names, PGM numbering concordances and apparatus. Described here at procedure-type level only.

publications.title: Techniques of Solomonic Magic
publications.publisher: Golden Hoard Press, Singapore, 2015; US trade edition Llewellyn
publications.whatItContains: The transmission argument proper: structural comparison of purification, circle construction, planetary day/hour election, suffumigation, evocation method, spirit hierarchies and implements across the Hygromanteia manuscript families and the Clavicula Salomonis families, arguing the former is the direct ancestor of the latter.

publications.title: The Magical Treatise of Solomon or Hygromanteia (trans. Ioannis Marathakis)
publications.note: Skinner's imprint published the first full English translation of the Hygromanteia; its subtitle — 'The True Ancestor of the Key of Solomon' — states the transmission claim on the cover. The subtitle is the publisher's/editor's framing and is reported as such.

proposedChannels: PGM (Graeco-Egyptian, 2nd c. BCE–5th c. CE) → late-antique/Byzantine Greek magical literature → Hygromanteia manuscript tradition (Byzantine, witnesses 15th–17th c., content argued older) → Clavicula Salomonis families (Latin/Italian/French/English, 15th–18th c.)

Evidence offered (per reviews and the thesis abstract): shared technique inventories, shared implement lists, shared structural sequences of operations, and manuscript-family stemmatics — NOT (per Harms's criticism, below) side-by-side collation of the actual prayers and invocations.

academicResponse.formalJournalReviewsLocated: NONE FOUND for either Techniques volume in Aries, Magic Ritual and Witchcraft, Correspondences, Ambix, Preternature, or La Rosa di Paracelso, after repeated targeted searching (July 2026). Skinner's own reviews page (sskinner.com/reviews.htm) likewise lists no academic-journal review of the magic corpus — only Amazon and trade reviews. This is an absence-of-located-evidence finding, not a proven absence.

positions.holder: Dan Harms (academic librarian, SUNY Cortland; grimoire bibliographer)
positions.venue: Papers Falling from an Attic Window (scholar-blog), review of Techniques of Graeco-Egyptian Magic, 12 Oct 2014, https://danharms.wordpress.com/2014/10/12/review-techniques-of-graeco-egyptian-magic/
positions.position: Positive with reservations: 'a welcome and significant addition to the literature', 'top-notch' for readers with the prerequisites (Betz to hand); praised the organisation of rituals by the papyri's own Greek/Demotic categories and the reference apparatus; faulted the opening chapter on defining magic for relying on dated sources.

positions.venue: Papers Falling from an Attic Window, review of Techniques of Solomonic Magic, 13 Jul 2015, https://danharms.wordpress.com/2015/07/13/review-techniques-of-solomonic-magic/
positions.position: On the thesis itself: the PGM → Hygromanteia → Clavicula lineage 'is not a new hypothesis', but Skinner is credited with systematically laying out the evidence by comparing the works. KEY CRITICISM: the book offers no comparison of the actual prayers and invocations between the corpora — precisely the parallel-passage philology that could establish transmission routes and date the changes. The evidentiary base is structural/typological, not textual collation.

positions.venue: 'Grimoires', in E. Asprem (ed.), Dictionary of Contemporary Esotericism, Leiden: Brill (preprint self-archived at ConTERN/CRESARCH, Aug 2018, https://contern.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/a-grimoires-lycourinos.pdf)
positions.position: Classifies Skinner (with Rankine) among 'scholar-magicians', distinguished from 'contemporary scholars' (Peterson, Harms, Lecouteux). Reports Skinner's position: the core of Western magic lies in the historical transmission of mainly Solomonic grimoires from Byzantium to Europe; magic remained a spiritual technology evolving from the PGM via the Hygromanteia, perpetuating a definitive Graeco-Egyptian operational rationale with the only major differences being the theological character of the spirits, the nomina, and the materia magica; and — decisively for reception — that 'Skinner seeks to restore the core of Western magic by tracing it back to its roots', i.e. the project has a stated restorative-practitioner aim, not only a historical one.

positions.holder: Egil Asprem, as cited by Lycourinos (same entry)
positions.venue: Asprem, 'Intermediary Beings', in C. Partridge (ed.), The Occult World, Routledge 2015, pp. 382–383, as cited in the Lycourinos entry
positions.position: The general caution set against grimoire-revival continuity claims: 'Despite contemporary claims of an unbroken tradition of Western magic, evidence is scant at times.' Lycourinos adds (citing Otto, Aries 16, 2016) that this does not mean no continuity whatsoever — books of magic from different periods inspire a continuity of praxis by later actors 'fleshing out' their contents. Position reported at second hand; Asprem's page-referenced text not independently checked.

positions.venue: 'The Study of Solomonic Magic in English' (long-running bibliographic survey; accessed via pdfcoffee mirror of the academia.edu text — mirror provenance caveat), https://www.academia.edu/4881091/The_Study_of_Solomonic_Magic_in_English
positions.position: Treats Techniques of Solomonic Magic as presenting Skinner's 'entire scholarly process' with its charts and tables, and as arguing a 'clear line of transmission from the Hygromanteia to the Clavicula Salomonis'; judges it likely to prove among the most significant works of its kind. One recorded quibble: Skinner's speculation about the angel name Zoharariel misreads merkavah-tradition evidence that predates the Zohar by centuries.

positions.venue: PhD in Classics awarded 2014 (repository record uon:13943)
positions.position: The one formal academic validation the thesis has received: it passed doctoral examination in a Classics program. No examiner reports are public.

academicResponse.statusForThisSite: The continuity thesis must be presented as a HYPOTHESIS with the following evidentiary status: (a) the Hygromanteia→Clavicula link is older scholarship that Skinner systematises rather than originates (so says Harms 2015, and the Marathakis translation the claim rides on is itself published by Skinner's own imprint); (b) the strongest documented criticism is that the argument is typological, not philological — no collation of parallel operative text is offered (Harms 2015); (c) no peer-reviewed journal review of either volume has been located; (d) the named field scholars (Kieckhefer, Klaassen, Page, Davies, Fanger, Otto, Faraone, Torallas Tovar, Peterson) have NOT been found engaging the thesis directly in print — reported as not-located, never as endorsement or rejection. Any repo edge citing Skinner for a PGM→grimoire transmission claim must carry claimedBy: Skinner (2014/2015) and this contested/uncorroborated status, per FRAMING §1.3 and §2.4.

part2_practitionerVsPhilologist.framing: Skinner publishes through both academic-adjacent form (PhD thesis, apparatus-heavy editions) and occult trade channels (his own Golden Hoard Press, Singapore; US trade editions with Llewellyn). The reception splits by audience, and the split is a documented fact about the field, not a verdict on him.

academicSideReception.point: The Brill dictionary entry's taxonomy is itself the reception datum: Skinner and Rankine are the type-specimens of the 'scholar-magician' category, credited with real manuscript research (British Library, Bodleian) and with publishing previously unpublished manuscripts, while being distinguished from the scholars proper.
academicSideReception.source: Lycourinos, 'Grimoires', Brill Dictionary of Contemporary Esotericism preprint (2018)

academicSideReception.point: Harms on the Skinner–Clark Ars Notoria (Golden Hoard, 2019; Llewellyn 2020, ISBN 978-0-7387-6452-8): praised the historical introduction, manuscript analysis and full-colour reproduction of Yale Beinecke Mellon MS 1; criticised (i) building the edition on Agrippa's Opera omnia Latin text (c. 1620) and Robert Turner's 1657 English translation rather than the medieval manuscripts, which diverge significantly; (ii) interpretive overreach — collapsing three candidate 'Euclids' into 'Euclid of Thebes' while conceding the attribution is weak, then indexing under it; (iii) speculative iconographic claims (notae linked to inverted Medusa heads in a Constantinople cistern) without adequate argument; (iv) transcription methodology and sparse apparatus in places.
academicSideReception.source: Harms, review of Ars Notoria: The Grimoire of Rapid Learning by Magic, 22 Feb 2020, https://danharms.wordpress.com/2020/02/22/review-ars-notoria-the-grimoire-of-rapid-learning-by-magic/

academicSideReception.point: The recurring academic-side pattern across reviews: apparatus, manuscript access, surveys of manuscript families and sheer usefulness are praised; the faulted elements are witness selection (early-modern printed texts over medieval manuscripts), single-reading interpretive choices, and speculative identifications.
academicSideReception.source: Synthesis of Harms 2014/2015/2020 and Karr (survey); each individual claim cited above

academicSideReception.point: Karr's comparative judgment keeps the philologist's benchmark elsewhere: Joseph Peterson's Lemegeton (Lesser Key of Solomon, Weiser 2001) is 'by far the best edition available of a complete Lemegeton' — while the Skinner–Rankine Goetia of Dr Rudd is valued for containing 'much material which no other version does' (Harley MS 6483, with Harley 6482, Sloane 3824, Wellcome MS 32). Complementary strengths, reported as positions.
academicSideReception.source: Karr, 'The Study of Solomonic Magic in English' (mirror caveat as above)

practitionerSideReception.point: Practitioner venues receive the Techniques volumes as authoritative and enabling. Spiral Nature's reviewer ('Frater 232', May 2016) calls Techniques of Solomonic Magic 'required reading for all practicing Solomonic mages' and — the load-bearing sentence for this repo — values it because the corpus-wide comparison lets practitioners 'fill in missing details and to combine techniques from multiple grimoires into a coherent whole'. He accepts the continuity argument as 'sound... based on extensive, well-documented research' while stating he lacks the expertise to verify it.
practitionerSideReception.repoRelevantNote: Practitioners explicitly read Skinner's comparative apparatus as a licence for cross-grimoire recombination and gap-filling — the exact completion-by-inference and aggregation moves FRAMING.md §5 A-1/A-2 forbid this site to make or facilitate. Skinner's reception is thus a live case study of why those rules exist.

practitionerSideReception.point: Techniques of Graeco-Egyptian Magic, practitioner reading: praised as making the PGM workable ('one can work with the PGM in ways that weren't possible before'), while noting it is 'no fluff — just facts, charts', disappointing spell-seekers.

The Sourceworks of Ceremonial Magic series (Skinner & Rankine, 6 vols 2004–2010: Practical Angel Magic of Dr John Dee's Enochian Tables; Keys to the Gateway of Magic; Goetia of Dr Rudd; Veritable Key of Solomon; Grimoire of St Cyprian – Clavis Inferni; A Cunning Man's Grimoire) is received in the community as the standard practitioner-facing manuscript-based corpus. Veritable Key of Solomon (Llewellyn ISBN 978-0-7387-1453-0): Kenneth Hite-authored LiveJournal review (princeofcairo, 9 Mar 2009) praises footnotes and the survey of the four Key families and fifteen text-groups, with the honest caveat that he 'can't vouch for the translation'.
practitionerSideReception.source: https://princeofcairo.livejournal.com/137833.html; series inventory per sskinner.com and trade records

practitionerSideReception.point: Skinner's own reviews page collects only Amazon, trade-magazine and community reviews — no academic journal notices for the magic titles. His prominence markers on the practitioner side are real and datable: Watkins 'Most Spiritually Influential Living People' list feature (2022), headline slots at practitioner conferences (e.g. Occulture), and a steady podcast/interview circuit.
practitionerSideReception.source: sskinner.com/reviews.htm (self-hosted aggregation); Wikipedia article citing Watkins Mind Body Spirit 2022; occultureconference.com speaker page
practitionerSideReception.provenance: self-reported (flagged), with independent trade-press corroboration for the Watkins listing

part2_practitionerVsPhilologist.tensionStatedNeutrally: The same features produce opposite valuations: corpus-wide tabulation of operative technique is, to the academic reviewers, a useful but philologically incomplete apparatus (no textual collation, contested witness choices); to the practitioner reviewers it is precisely what makes the corpus operable again. Lycourinos records that the restorative aim is Skinner's own stated framing, not an accusation. The site reports this tension as a documented feature of contemporary grimoire scholarship.

part3_geomancyAndFengShui.claim: The geomancy scholarship is the most academically respected part of the corpus; the feng shui compass work has also drawn genuine academic-journal review. Both are documented below with the actual citations.

items.work: Terrestrial Astrology: Divination by Geomancy, London: Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1980, xiii + 293 pp., ISBN 0-7100-0553-9 (revised/reissued as Geomancy in Theory and Practice, Golden Hoard)

reception.venue: Medical History 26:1 (1982), pp. 107–108 (peer-reviewed journal; open access at PMC1139129)
reception.content: Chief merit, in the reviewer's words: it 'has brought together versions of geomancy described in various eastern and western cultures, studied separately but never compared before'. Criticism: Skinner failed to use — or even list — Wellcome MSS 10 (Gerard of Cremona's 'Geomantiae astronomicae'), 394 (Phillippus von Schlammersdorf Knodius) and 531 ('Geomantia edita a magistro Gerardo Cremonensi'). Verdict: 'a very informative book on a little-known subject'. The review also records the book's transmission argument: an Arabian origin (Persia, India and Palestine dismissed 'with good reasons'), spreading by three routes — across North Africa to the Sahara; via the Red Sea and Indian Ocean to Madagascar; via Muslim Spain to the rest of Europe — and notes Robert Fludd's own name for the art, 'terrestrial astrology'.
reception.provenance: peer-reviewed-journal (full text verified from the PMC scan, July 2026)

items.standing: Publisher and community copy describe it as the first and still most complete English-language history of Western divinatory geomancy; that superlative is trade framing and is labelled as such. Its diffusion chapters continue to be cited in academic literature on Islamic and African geomancy (e.g. by Wim van Binsbergen's geomancy papers), but the specific citing sentences were NOT verified this session — recorded as unresolved rather than asserted.

items.work: Guide to the Feng Shui Compass: A Compendium of Classical Feng Shui, Singapore: Golden Hoard, 2008, 448 pp., ISBN 978-0-9547639-9-2

reception.venue: East Asian Science, Technology, and Medicine (EASTM) 37 (2013), review beginning p. 111 (Brill; ISSN 1562-918X)
reception.content: Opens with strong praise — 'Stephen Skinner is probably the most important Western scholar taking the science of Fengshui serious[ly]', crediting him with clarifying feng shui's 'rather vague image' in the West over decades. The review's critical remarks (per its abstract; full text behind paywall this session): the later sections become overly technical without clear guidance, and there are issues with the sourcing of traditional Chinese texts, inaccuracies in some geographic claims, and questionable choices of example illustrations.
reception.provenance: peer-reviewed-journal (opening praise quoted in secondary aggregations and Wikipedia; critical detail from the review's abstract — full text not accessed, flagged)

items.standing: The book is the first English-language monograph-length treatment of the luopan (75 rings catalogued) — a publisher's claim (self-reported) that the EASTM review's existence partially corroborates in significance if not in wording.

items.work: Early feng shui corpus (The Living Earth Manual of Feng-Shui, 1976, and successors; Feng Shui for Modern Living magazine, 1998–; Feng Shui History)
items.reception: Mass-market reception (trade reviews, Amazon); the magazine's 2000 PPA Publisher of the Year nomination is reported by Skinner's own site. No academic review located for the popular titles; classed as trade output. Provenance: self-reported.

unresolved: No review of Techniques of Graeco-Egyptian Magic or Techniques of Solomonic Magic located in Aries, Magic Ritual and Witchcraft, Correspondences, Ambix, Preternature or La Rosa di Paracelso. Absence of located reviews is not proof none exist — Brill/Project MUSE review sections are poorly indexed by open search.

Direct engagement (positive or negative) with Skinner's continuity thesis by Kieckhefer, Klaassen, Page, Davies, Fanger, Otto, Faraone, Torallas Tovar or Peterson: none located in openly accessible text this session. Whether Otto's 'Historicising Western Learned Magic' (Aries 16, 2016, pp. 161–240) cites Skinner could not be checked (paywalled).
Full text of Theobald's EASTM 37 (2013) review not accessed (Brill 403); its critical points are taken from the review's published abstract and must be re-verified before any page-cited use.

The van Binsbergen geomancy papers' handling of Terrestrial Astrology (authoritative vs merely listed) unverified — the 1996 Binghamton paper PDF was retrieved but its bibliography could not be text-extracted this session (saved to tool-results for a future pass).
An academia.edu-posted review of the Skinner–Clark Ars Notoria (2019) exists (id 40612839); its author and venue were not identifiable (403 + mirror served only the book's own introduction).
Skinner's PhD supervisors and examiners: not publicly recorded in the repository metadata fetched.
Exact end-page of the Theobald review and of the EASTM citation (37:1, 2013, pp. 111–ff.).
risks: LIVING PERSON: all characterisations above are tied to named reviewers and venues; the 'scholar-magician' label is Lycourinos's published classification, not this site's judgment; the restorative-practitioner aim is reported by Lycourinos as Skinner's own framing. No motive, belief or finance speculation is included and none may be added downstream.

The continuity thesis maps onto exactly the transmission edges the repo's operative graph models. If any edge cites Skinner, it must carry claimedBy with year and locus, the Harms not-new/not-collated caveats as a second position, and must never be flattened into background fact (FRAMING §1.3, §2.4).

Practitioner reception documents cross-grimoire recombination as the community's USE of Skinner's apparatus — quoting that reception on-site must not itself model or endorse the recombination move (FRAMING §5 A-1/A-2). Describe the reception; do not reproduce the method.

Provenance skew: the academic-side record rests heavily on one credentialed blogger (Harms) plus one Brill reference-entry preprint; treating these as 'the academic consensus' would overstate. State venue class wherever cited.

Two sources were accessed via mirrors (Karr survey via pdfcoffee; Lycourinos via author's self-archived preprint) — published versions may differ; re-verify wording before any on-site quotation-free paraphrase is attributed with page numbers.

Several superlatives in circulation ('first English book on...', 'most complete work on...', 'world's leading expert') trace to publisher copy or Skinner's own site; each is labelled self-reported here and must stay labelled.
Copyright: everything Skinner has published is in copyright; this dossier contains bibliographic description and short attributed reviewer phrases only, and no text of his editions.
